04 · Multiprocessor Scheduling

Multiprocessor/Multicore Scheduling

  • Classifications of Multiprocessor Systems:

    • Loosely Coupled/Distributed Microprocessors or cluster processors:
      • Consists of a collection of relatively autonomous systems, each processor having its own main memory and I/O channels
    • Functionally specialized processor:
      • There is a primary, general-purpose processor
      • Specialized processors are generally controlled by the primary processor, and provide services to it
    • Tightly Coupled Multiprocessors:
      • Consists of a set of processors that share common main memory and are under the integrated control of the OS
      • Symmetrical MultiProcessing (SMP) is the most common modern example of this

  • Synchronization granularity in processes

    Grain Size Description Sync Interval (instructions)
    Fine Parallelism inherent in a single instruction stream < 20
    Medium Parallel processing or multitasking within a single application 20 – 200
    Coarse Multiprocessing of concurrent processes in a multiprogrammed env. 200 – 2,000
    Very Coarse Distributed processes across network nodes 2,000 – 1M
    Independent Multiple unrelated processes N/A

  • Independent Parallelism

    • No explicit synchronization between processes
      • Each process represents a separate, independent job or application
      • Typically used in time-sharing systems where each user is (generally) performing an independent job
    • Multiprocessor provides the same service as a multiprogrammed uniprocessor
    • Because there are multiple processors, average user response time is lower

  • Coarse/Very Coarse:

    • There is synchronization between processes, but at a very low level
    • Easily handled as a set of concurrent processes running on a multiprogrammed processor
    • Can be supported on a multiprocessor with little to no change in user software

  • Medium-Grained Parallelism

    • Single application can be effectively implemented as a collection of threads within a single process
      • Programmer must explicitly specify the potential parallelism in code
      • There needs to be a high-degree of coordination and interaction among threads of an application
    • Because the various threads of an application interact so frequently, scheduling decisions concerning one thread may affect the performance of the entire application
      • Think of if a single thread gets blocked, and the others don’t wait, which could cause data inconsistency

  • Fine-Grained Parallelism

    • Represents a much more complex use of parallelism than is found in the use of threads in code
    • Mostly OS/Scheduler, or hardware based

  • Design issues:

    • The approach taken to scheduling depends on a couple of things:
      • The granularity of applications
      • Speed of applications
      • The number of processors you have available
    • Scheduling on a multiprocessor involves three interrelated issues:
      • The dispatching of a process (separate but linked to the assignment of a process)
      • Assignment of processes to processors
      • Use of multiprogramming on an individual proccesor/core

  • Assignment of processes to a processor:

    • Assuming all processors are equal, it is simplest to treat processors like a pooled resource and assign processes to processors as needed
      • Dynamic Assignment
    • If a process is permanently assigned to a processor from activation to termination
      • Static Assignment
      • Each processor has its own short term assignment queue
      • The advantage is that there may be less overhead in the scheduling function
      • Allows for group/gang scheduling
      • Disadvantage:
        • Load imbalance: One processor could be idle, with an empty queue, while another processor has a backlog
        • The simplest solution is to provide a common queue of processes shared across all processors, or use dynamic load balancing

  • There are two methods of process assignment to a processor used for both static and dynamic methods:

    • Primary/Secondary Architecture
    • Peer Assignment

  • Primary Secondary Architecture

    • Primary processor executes key kernel functions, and schedules for all other processors
    • Secondary processors provides services for the primary
    • Think of the primary as the brain, and secondary as arms or legs
    • Advantages:
      • Simple, and requires very little enhancement to a multiprogrammed uniprocessor system
      • Conflict resolution for resources and synchronization is simplified since one processor has control
    • Disadvantage:
      • Single point of failure: If the primary fails, the system fails
      • Primary can become a performance bottleneck: If a lot of small processes are sent to schedule at the same time, it would take longer to distribute each task to a processor than it would take for that processor to complete that task

  • Peer Architecture:

    • Kernel can execute on any processor
    • Each processor does self-scheduling from a pool of available processes
    • Complicates the OS:
      • OS must ensure that two processors do not choose the same process, and that processes are completed before being removed from the queue

  • Process Scheduling:

    • In traditional multicore systems, processes are not dedicated to a single processor. Dynamic Assignment is most common.
    • A single process queue is used for all processors to retrieve tasks from
      • If some priority scheme is used, there are multiple queues, one for each priority

  • Thread Scheduling:

    • Thread execution is separated from the rest of a process
    • An application can be a set of threads that cooperate and execute concurrently (or in parallel) in the same memory address space
    • On a uniprocessor (concurrent system), threads can be used as a program structuring aid, and allows overlap of I/O processing
    • In a multiprocessor system, threads can be used to exploit true parallelism of an application
      • Dramatic gains in performance are possible in multiprocessor system due to this
    • Four approaches to thread scheduling:
      • Load sharing: Threads are not assigned to a particular processor
      • Gang Scheduling: A set of related threads are scheduled to run on a set of processors at the same time on a one-to-one basis
      • Dedicated Processor Assignment: Provides implicit scheduling defined by the assignment of threads to processors
      • Dynamic Scheduling: The number of threads in a process can be altered during the course of execution

  • Load Sharing:

    • Simplest approach and the one that carries over the most from uniprocessor environments
    • Advantages:
      • Load is distributed evenly across all processors, ensuring that no processor is idle while there is work available to do
      • No centralized scheduler required
      • There is a global queue of threads that is easier to organize and access
    • Disadvantages:
      • Central queue occupies a region of memory that must be accessed in a manner that enforces mutual exclusion (so multiple processors can’t take the same process)
        • Leads to performance bottleneck
      • Preemptive threads are unlikely to resume execution on the same processor
        • Caching becomes less efficient, leading to another performance bottleneck
      • If all threads are treated as a common pool of threads, it is unlikely that all of the threads of a program will gain access to processors at the same time
        • Decreases efficiency of parallel processes
        • The process switches could seriously compromise performance
    • Common implementations of Load sharing:
      • FCFS
      • Smallest number of threads first
      • Preemptive smallest number of threads first

  • Gang/Group Scheduling:

    • A set of related threads is scheduled to run on a set of processors at the same time on a one-to-one basis
    • Can be uniform or weighted:
      • Uniform: As processes have no weight, all the threads in one process will execute before the threads of another process, alternating until completion
      • Weighted: Processes are prioritized such that all of the threads of a higher priority process will execute until completion before another process executes
    • Advantages:
      • Synchronization and blocking may be reduced, as there is less process switching
      • Scheduling process overhead may be reduced
      • Useful for medium/fine grained applications whose performance severely degrades when any part of the application is not running, while other parts are ready to run
    • Disadvantage:
      • If there is a large process queue, a process will likely take longer to execute while waiting for processors to be freed for each of its threads

  • Dedicated processor assignment:

    • When an application is scheduled, each of its threads is assigned to a processor that remains dedicated to that thread until the application is completed
    • If a thread of an application is blocked waiting for I/O or for synchronization with another thread then that thread’s processor remains idle
    • Defense of this strategy:
      • In a highly parallel system with tens or hundreds of processors, processor utilization is no longer an important metric of a system
      • The total avoidance of process switching during the lifetime of a process should result in a substantial speedup of that process

Dynamic Scheduling

  • This method allows an application to adjust the number of threads used during execution
  • This allows the OS to adjust the load on processors to improve utilization by reallocating resources based on current workload
  • When a job requests one or more processors (either when the job arrives for the first time, or because its requirements change):
    • If there are idle processors, use them to satisfy the request
    • If there are no idle processors, and if the job making the request is a new arrival:
      • allocate a single processor by taking one away from any current job that currently holds more than one processor
    • If any portion of the request cannot be satisfied (if all current processes only have a single processor), the new job remains outstanding until either a processor becomes available, or the job is rescinded
